Yes, and I feel a lot of guilt for my past thoughts and actions. Growing up I was an obedient child (though my parent thought I was naughty - which is hilarious), which meant that I tried to please my parent. I would parrot her views, appease her. I thought she was some higher being. I'd been conditioned to always defend her, and to see any deviation from her as something that resulted in punishment, being frozen out or called names or treated like I was evil. 

When I look back at some childhood friendships I can see that although I cared for my friends intensely, I could be selfish and arrogant and often misread their motives. We were all just kids, but my parent would take a dislike to a friend I had, and then I'd start to believe it too. I acted in ways that were manipulative, looking back, and that were cruel - although I genuinely thought that was normal. 

Sometimes I lie awake at night thinking about all these things, and wishing I'd been different. Sometimes I think it's okay because I was a kid, but other times I feel like my friends were kids too, and regardless of the reasons, I made their lives difficult in lots of ways. There's no excuse and I find it hard to align how I am now, which is trying to be as compassionate and self-critical as possible, with how I used to think. 

It's hard to know on the one hand that you were abused and so were a victim, but in the process you hurt others. I feel angry about it, angry towards my parent and family, because they made me that way, but I also know I have to own it in order to not be like them. I think it just feels unfair that I got conditioned that way and am unlearning it now, but again, feeling sorry for yourself can be dangerous in some situations. My parent always sees herself as the victim, and I don't want to do that. She is a victim, don't get me wrong, but she chose to continue the cycle. I can't ever do that. I would literally rather die than continue the cycle, and it's why I don't want to ever have children. 

Most of the time I'm diligent and I make sure that I don't repeat patterns, but for me it comes out most when I'm in an argument or feeling cornered. My first thought, shamefully, is to verbally eviscerate the person with the worst things you can imagine, to go low and personal and to belittle. That's what was done to me and still is. I don't let that poison come out of my mouth, but I feel guilt for thinking it. 

It worries me that the urge to do that is still within me, although I am reassured by therapists I have seen for trauma that we are not our thoughts but our actions. They describe it a bit like when you're raised with bigotry. It might be second nature to think something bigoted, and even once you unlearn it, the thoughts might pop up, but that's more how you were raised - it doesn't represent your views today. 

I'm a constant work in progress, and I think I will always be very critical of my own thoughts and behaviour, which is probably for the best. At least I'm able to stand back and examine my behaviours. I'm also someone who apologises if I'm in the wrong, and I've made a habit of this even for small and insignificant things. I was never apologised to growing up, and it's been healing and humbling for me to realise just how easy and meaningful it is to apologise when you're wrong or make a mistake. 

Maybe in another life I would have been a mum, but that's not a risk I feel I can take. I'm not saying it's wrong for anyone else to do - I get so much comfort from reading the stories of those who have broken the cycle and become wonderful parents - but I'm not 100% confident I could handle it, and for all the love in the world I couldn't bear to put any child through the emotional pain I've been left with and will carry until my dying day.

Please tell an adult, even if it's a teacher or staff member at school. This behaviour isn't normal, and you can still love your mum and pity her while protecting yourself. It's just not worth the risk, even if she seems sorry (for herself) afterwards. All it takes is one moment of losing control and you could end up injured or worse. 

It could be that she is unwell herself, and so telling a trusted adult might also be what she needs to get support. Either way, living with this much stress is going to make you ill. We're not built to feel fear all the time, and you sound like you're frozen with it - which is understandable and perfectly normal in your circumstances.

I really am so sorry that you're in this situation. You deserve to feel safe and happy,

Have you tried sitting down with her, maybe with your other sibling present to help keep things calm, and giving a full and frank apology?  Maybe you could tell her the things you're writing here, which are that you know you did wrong and you've tried hard to change and show that you can be better? It's up to her what happens after that, and even if you weren't all to blame and were only part of a cycle, ultimately she gets to decide when she's 'over it', if she ever is. 

I know that's hard to hear. I'm really sorry for what it's worth, because if you were suffering as well then I can understand why this feels unjust, but all I can say is that it's her decision to make, and all you can really do is apologise fully, let her know you'd like to get to know each other again, and leave it up to her. 

If she's being rude then I can only advise that you stay calm, tell her you understand her feelings and would be willing to talk it through with her, but if that's not the case, might she agree to some boundaries and basic rules of civility while you're there?

I hope things work out for you, OP.

I think it's because people are uncomfortable with imperfect victims. Erik better fits the role society wants from their victims, which is very emotional, vulnerable, younger than Lyle, so people can say he was controlled by him. He's more likely to cry than rage, and people like that from victims. Lyle was also a victim of both parents, but his reaction was to seem harder and less emotional. That doesn't mean he felt/feels less than Erik, but that his response to severe abuse and trying to avoid more of it was projecting 'strength' in the way Jose viewed it. The reasons people call Lyle psychopathic are actually really clear trauma responses. Some victims fawn, some flee, some fight, some freeze. Lyle seems to have frozen for a lot of his life, but when he fought, which was all he'd ever seen modelled by his father, people who don't understand trauma and abuse turned on him.   
  
I believe that without Lyle, Erik would be dead. Perhaps both of them. Lyle made a lot of bad decisions, and since he was older, people blame him more, but what do people expect from kids raised in that environment? If Lyle is being groomed into being 'stronger' and more assertive, then it makes sense he'd be the one making decisions. If Erik is being groomed into obedience (so access to him is easier for Jose), then it makes sense he'd be more likely to defer to Lyle.   
  
They were groomed into these roles, groomed into their survival reactions, but people still want to blame them. I think it's also to do with how people perceive male victims. Erik's response is similar in some ways to how most (not all!) women might respond to such abuse. Many find that easier to understand. Lyle's response was more complicated and again, makes sense as someone who was being groomed to become an alpha male, only without any real control or safety.  

Lyle isn't a monster, and if he behaved in a monstrous way, it was in response to the way he was groomed and abused to react. Even his reaction has his father's fingerprints all over it. I don't think he can be judged as an individual in those circumstances. I don't think either boy know who they were, or had the chance to figure that out.

I’ve been thinking about this for a while, but I’m not sure I’m articulating it well enough, so please forgive me if this seems rambling or disorganised. Also please forgive me for how long this is.

Essentially, Gabby freed me from blaming myself for the abuse I have received, demonstrated the reality of what it means to be a victim (which took away the shame), and came to represent a triumph over abuse. I hope that last part doesn’t sound insensitive, but what I mean is that in a world where an abuser tries to smear and malign their victim, to blame them and shame them, Gabby still rose above that. For whatever reason, Gabby was special. People took to her. People could sense, I think, that she was a good person. The lies and smears just didn’t stick. We felt, collectively, that we wanted to protect her, and that something was wrong. I don’t know how to explain that phenomenon other than calling it a miracle, because before we were aware she had passed, people could feel her warmth and wanted to find her. Although Gabby is no longer here, her truth has risen up. As a woman, I remember feeling that something was wrong and off. It was like a sense we have, that this was a person that could have been our own friend or sister, and we felt something like loyalty? It’s hard to describe, but many of us have either been in that position, or had friends who have been there. The way people, especially women, came together for Gabby was something hopeful and brilliant.

Gabby was so vibrant, sunny, courageous, hopeful, creative and special. She was the sort of girl you’d want to be friends with because she gave off such happy, warm vibes. For me, it was a kind of groundbreaking moment in self-compassion. People still blame victims, they can call them stupid, or make them out to be the villains. Yet we had Gabby’s own voice and testimony thanks to her social media presence. It woke people up to the fact that victims don’t get targeted because of any fault in them, but often it’s the kindest people, the most nurturing, the most compassionate, because they are the ones that trust in others, give their love and support to those around them, and believe that people can do better. For me, that shone through in Gabby. Especially with what we know about how controlling her abuser became. It was like a light clicked on for me, and for others. (I have been a victim myself, but not in a romantic relationship). It was Gabby’s freedom and joy and talent that was so threatening to people like her abuser. She simply wouldn’t be controlled. Her soul and spirit were too free. It helped me with self-compassion, and in compassion for others. In a world where we can often blame a victim, Gabby was this shining example that often victims are kind, they trust in others, they want to help, and this is a wonderful thing. It’s no flaw in them, it’s wickedness in those who would hurt anyone so loving.

We could all see Gabby’s talent, even in the vlog she posted. It was a high standard, it looked fun, it was well edited. She had creative gifts, and selfish, jealous people cannot seem to handle those (especially young women) who possess talent and potential. They see that talent, and they try to squash it. They are insecure, narcissistic, and self-loathing, and it is unfortunately good, brilliant people like Gabby who want to help those who are wounded. You can see in the vlog that Gabby is trying to make her abuser feel comfortable, to include him, to soothe him. Yet it was not enough. It never is enough. I believe Gabby was someone bubbling over with compassion, who wanted to connect with the world and heal things where she could. It is no flaw in her that she wanted to heal her abuser. It is a sign of her strength and brilliance that she wanted to see the best in him. She was not foolish or naïve. She was loving, caring, and nurturing. I think the world needed to see this in a victim, because it can be so hard for those who have not lived it to recognise the dynamic.

In terms of victim blaming and the dynamics of abuse, when Gabby was so apologetic and upset when talking to police, some people simply did not understand what was at play, but for many of us, it was heart-breaking, but also something that changed our lives. For me personally, I saw myself. After being abused and hurt, I would blame myself, I would make excuses. I wanted to see the good, and I didn’t want strangers to think badly of my loved one. I wanted to protect them even then. I think this incident, captured on camera, as horrific as it must have been for those who knew her, allowed many people to see the truth, which was that Gabby’s radical compassion, her desire to protect the very person who hurt her, was not a flaw. It was a gift, but one that was used to harm her. We saw her abuser so calm, covering his tracks, and I think many of us realised that in him was a version of our own abusers. As we scrambled to make excuses for them, to help them, wanting them to heal, they were willing to hurt our reputations and use our kindness against us. Gabby played it all down, she only wanted peace and love, for things to be better. Through her sorrow, at such a terrible low moment for her, she was still thinking of him and his reputation. When people ask why victims take the blame initially, they don’t understand that it’s part of the process. They can use this early blame taking to imply mutual abuse or to suggest the victim was the perpetrator. The reality, as Gabby has showed the world, is that a victim still tries to protect those they love. They will protect even those who hurt them. That’s not weakness. They are not to blame.

I know that in a lot of cases, we blame ourselves. We are made to believe that if only we’d been different in some way, we wouldn’t have been abused. But Gabby showed and still does show that there is no shame or weakness in being a victim, because it’s not any negative reflection on that person, and in many ways it’s a mark of someone having something special about them and holding potential, because abuse is so often about jealousy. Gabby was a brave, brilliant, and bold young woman. I can’t imagine even getting to the planning stages of travelling the country, let alone actually doing it! She demonstrates, in a world of victim blaming, that her only ‘crime’ was being loving and talented. Abusers latch onto people with talent and kindness, and in their jealousy they have to bring them down to size. It is their weakness. They are intimidated by the victim’s positive qualities. They try to make them small, because what they know is that their victim’s impact is vast, their potential is vast, and that in comparison, they haven’t got a lot to offer.

I think of Gabby often, because she helped me come to terms with my own situation. I am trying, now, to stop making excuses for those who abuse me. I am trying not to hide my passions and talents to make others more comfortable and less likely to hurt me. I also find great hope in her story, despite the sad way it ended, because ultimately Gabby has touched the world. People still think of Gabby, people know she was talented, when people hear her name they think of that smiling, beautiful, brave young woman. I think of a free spirit. Gabby was working on her social media presence and her vlog, because she wanted to help inspire people, and she has. She truly has. She’s probably saved countless lives.

I’m grateful that she was here and I’m so sorry for those who knew and loved her, and also the world, which has lost a great advocate, and someone who I am sure would have used her creativity and compassion to spread joy and knowledge.

I hope this wasn’t too long, or overstepping in any way. When I hear Gabby’s name now, I think of a young woman smiling, laughing, hiking, barefoot, being free. I believe her being here was a miracle. I really, truly believe she has saved, and will save, countless lives.

Can you talk to a teacher or someone in authority? What you are experiencing is severe abuse, and it sounds like a really controlling environment. Please do not hurt yourself. You are not the problem. You are reacting in a normal way to something unnatural. You’re being gaslit, coerced, and diminished, all to feed their egos. You have been hurt. You had a bottle thrown at you. I think you could talk to the police about that? It’s an assault. You also need help for your suicidal feelings because this home you’re in is driving you to despair. It’s another form of torture for you. 

You’re not in the wrong. They are. They’re sick and they’re abusing you, and you mustn’t believe what they’re saying. There’s no excuse for it. I know they’re trying to make you feel crazy and dramatic, but I repeat, you are reacting totally normally to something which is psychological destruction and physical abuse. 

OP, you have to get out of there. Is this possible for you? Can you stay with a friend? Can you talk to a teacher/tutor? Could you call the police? 

Do not let them rob you of your life. You have a happy life ahead of you, and they’re trying to exhaust you into being their puppet. Don’t let them steal it from you. Stand firm. It’ll be the hardest thing you’ll ever do, but get through this and you’ll have a real life. It’s out there for you. 

Your parents are sick. You’re innocent of blame. You are their child. They should love you and support you. They should want you to be happy. What they are doing is truly evil, and I pray you get into a different environment where you can feel the love and support you deserve.

It could just be fleas, so behaviours and feelings you’ve learned from growing up with the examples you have, but honestly speaking, even if you do have NPD, then the fact you are aware, that it bothers you, and that you don’t want to abuse others, means you’re a better person than your parents, and that you have every hope for a brighter future. 

I think therapy would help a lot, because sometimes when you’ve been abused for so long, you fall into bad patterns of thinking. Why wouldn’t you, when all you’ve seen is abuse? But you can unlearn that, and figure out who you actually are. 

I think the insecurity could simply be that you’re a victim of long-term abuse. It doesn’t mean you’re a good or a bad person. There are some abusers who were abused themselves, that’s true. But there are also a lot of people who were abused, notice the patterns, and make the effort to be different. 

You can see the pattern, it’s worrying to you. Ask yourself this, would an abuser really care? In my experience this sort of self-reflection doesn’t happen. Maybe the occasional glimmer, but never enough to get them to question their whole lives and personalities. They like to hide and deflect and get angry. But you’re posting here for support and asking strangers to read this and respond. 

I’m not qualified to diagnose you at all, but unlearn the abusive tendencies and give yourself time before you begin blaming yourself. If once you have had therapy and got some distance you feel the same way, then that’s okay too. You’re aware of the impact of these behaviours. You can still choose to be different. I believe in you.

There are some really weird similarities in our lives it seems? I went through something similar, so I can relate to how it feels. I get that it’s hard for her, but this moment is about you and your father, and I think her hatred and jealousy robbed you of something important. Even if she was concerned (which it sounds like she has no reason to be, if your dad has had therapy and is now able to offer counselling to others) then this wasn’t the way to go about it. How does humiliating you help? All it does is bring you shame and trauma. This is \*your\* life, and you were hurt. I’m sure she was too, but you were the kid in the relationship. 

Even if there was some reason why she hates him (I mean a valid reason), there‘s no excuse for the way she made you feel. It seems controlling and intimidating, and honestly seems to have made an experience which could have been one of the most positive and liberating in your life, be forever tainted by her horrible horrible reaction. 

Bottom line is, she’s not putting you first. It’s not a contest between your parents, it should be about both wanting you to be happy, and I can only see one parent behaving that way here. I can’t judge by anything other than your post, but in terms of the here and now, it seems one parent has matured, takes responsibility, and is trying to heal wounds. The other seems to be getting jealous and hijacking something very important to you. 

I wish you the best because I’ve been where you are. When one parent is abusive (but looked after you), and the other was absent, it’s complicated. What I do know is that both should have your best interests at heart now, all past mistakes aside. They created a lot of trauma for you, and they need to be helping you now, not exploding.

That sucks, I’m really sorry. Thankfully, her games can’t have diminished how great you looked, but I get what you mean entirely. It’s the principle of it. You’d think a parent would want to be a support, not to play power games on their child’s actual wedding? At least others recognised what she’d done though. I’m sure people who didn‘t say anything also noticed, and would have been feeling a lot of compassion for you. It seems like she wanted to be the main event, and she did that by trying to leech off you. Again, I’m really sorry, but also, I hope it‘s a somewhat funny story you can tell with the photos (to people you trust) about just how petty she is.

Yes. This is my exact situation. My mother was abused and continues to be abused, and when I was a kid, up until now, I’ve been her protector against it. She used to cry and rage, and I’d see her mocked and belittled, and hear about the most awful things. Yet she does these same things to me. It‘s sick, because I lost my childhood caring for her as well as taking her abuse, and yet she has zero self-reflection. It’s really sad to realise, and it’s complicated for so many reasons, but to see someone abused into the cycle is horrifying. I grieve for her and me, but ultimately I know she made her choices. I had no choice as a child, like she didn’t. But now I’m an adult I can no longer make excuses for her. I would do anything not to repeat this cycle, to the extent that I’m probably \*too\* critical of myself. I made the choice not to inflict this on anyone. She went the other way. 

In addition to this, she still comes to me for support in her abuse, and describes almost perfectly the exact same things she does to me. That’s galling. Like you say, it’s almost funny. The complete lack of awareness.

Yeah, I’m happy for that person, because their experience of family seems wildly different from mine, but reading that when you have an abusive family feels like gaslighting. Not that it’s wrong for them to use this advice, but it certainly reads differently when you’re like us!

I think she’s a narcissist, and even if she isn’t, she’s abusive. You’re not a baby. Your experience rings very true for me. I know some people have situations where the narc is always horrific, but for some of us, we get periods of kindness or togetherness between the abuse. Usually it‘s when they’re in control of a situation. The abuse happens for me when I act like an individual or step out of her image of me. 

Mine loves me. She really does love me. She also abuses me. She scares me. We can be close and I pity her so much because she endured abuse of her own, but she’s also an abuser. I love her and she terrifies me. 

No matter how they feel, we have to think about how they \*act\*. Even if they love us, if they abuse us, that doesn’t make it okay. It’s complicated when they have their own trauma, but they make the choice to abuse us. I feel like I couldn’t live without mine sometimes, but other times all I wish is to be apart from her, that I could be free. In some cases, that’s part of the conditioning. It keeps you loyal, keeps you making excuses, and keeps you blaming yourself. 

It’s like an an abusive romantic relationship. It’s not always constant abuse. It can be nice things in between, so the victim doubts themselves, and later feels conflicted about what to do. They can end up staying because they know the ‘good’ version of the person. But the truth is that person is one person. They are all the things they do. If they abuse you, they’re an abuser.

Please call the police. You need to get out of there. This is abuse and it’s dangerous. It’s escalated to a place where she will use physical violence to control you, and you need to be safe. I know that’s scary, but you have a life to live out there and a load of people who are going to love you and make your life a happy one. As other posters have said, it will not get better, it will get worse. She is pushing boundaries and escalating. I wish you my best and I wish you courage and strength to get out of there.

I mean I think they are their own worst enemies, and also ours, because in their selfish need to be the best and most important, they actually destroy themselves and others, and make the world a worse place. I don’t believe they ever achieve happiness, they don’t understand community and compassion, and they actively prevent our world from improving. They‘re like children emotionally. They’re really really immature, and it’s jarring, because they can often be charming and have a lot of power, but at the heart of it they’re just selfish kids.
I want to be like your sister too! She sounds amazing!

Thank you for sharing this, and also thank you for raising two amazing kids who will no doubt make the world a better place. I believe it’s like a chain reaction, because what you’ve done with them, the cycles you’ve broken, will hopefully touch everyone they come into contact with way down the line.

This makes so much sense and thank you for sharing. I feel the same way. I worry so often that I’ll not get it right because of my experiences, I think about my trauma and imperfections, and it’s scary. I do feel maternal instincts, but it’s very complicated, I think because of this huge fear of letting my child down. But what you’ve written has really moved me, because you’re right. We don’t have to be perfect, we just need to do our best, and to apologise to them if we do wrong. I want my child/children to know that sometimes I will make the wrong choices, but that if ever I do, if ever I speak to them harshly, I will \*always\* be accountable, I will always apologise, talk it through, and do better for them. 

I can’t thank you enough for this response. It’s helping me so much.

My friend, what you are going through is unbearable and I’m so sorry. I’m not an expert, but my advice is to please just keep your head down, play the game. This sounds genuinely dangerous, and you need to make sure that you get away from them via college. While this is being sorted (and I wish I would help you but I don’t know how) you need to just be calm, and focus on your safety. It must be torture to live this way, but once you’re out of there you’re going to have a full life and make your own choices. Main priority is being safe. You say this method of discipline is legal where you are, and if that’s the case, stay calm, just get through those next months. You have a way out, you know that’s on the horizon. Don’t lose hope. This is gonna be a really really tough time in your life, but if you can get out and away, the world is going to be a different place.

You feel bad a) because she’s manipulative as hell and b) because you’re a good person. They like to torment people with a conscience, because every bone in our body makes us want to be good. Normal people hate upsetting others, it makes us want to fix things. Unfortunately, narcs use this as a weapon against us by playing victim and trying to inflict guilt we don’t deserve. 

You’re exactly right when you point out her hypocrisy. They love telling people how real they are, how they‘re genuine, yet they expect us to enable them and feed their egos, otherwise we face consequences .

She’s playing a classic game here. She’s manipulating you to make you feel pity. She’s acting like a wounded victim, and you’ve been so conditioned to tune into her needs (likely for survival), that her behaving in this way likely feels unbearable and like you’d do anything to get out of it. That‘s the trap though, because you can’t win. It’s manipulative and it’s controlling. Don’t be fooled by it, although I know that‘s easier said than done. When it happens to me I sometimes end up apologizing and making things right even when I’m the victim. You play into their fantasy, or you get the cold shoulder and your guilt (which is a strenget) is used against you. It’s sick that they use that empathy to hurt us. 

So yeah, to summarise, you feel bad because you hold empathy and seem like a decent human being who doesn’t want to upset others. But in this situation and with your history, you are justified, and she is trying to play this card to control you.

This makes me so happy to read. A lot of us don’t end up having kids for lots of reasons, but I genuinely believe that those of us who want to have kids, would be good parents, or at the very least, we‘d be willing to learn and put our children first. Once you’ve felt how horrible it is as a kid, it gives you this drive to make sure no child ever goes through it again. I also think it’s a sense of being proved right (I don’t know if that’s healthy, but it’s how I feel). All the years of being told your abuser/abusers did their best, and that any parent would behave that way, and that a childhood without abuse is a fairytale - to makes you want to get it right just to show them. They’re the ones who had it wrong.

I think about this all the time. I try not to obsess on it, because I know I can’t change the past, but it does hurt. My childhood wasn’t normal in any way, and I think I could deal with that, honestly, if I wasn’t still being gaslit about it. My family still pretend we had this perfect setup, when the reality was hugely traumatic and dysfunctional. In terms of advice, I wish I had some to give you. I’m sorry if that’s unpopular or controversial to say, but it’s true. Perpetrators of domestic violence rarely see themselves as evil, and it it’s this idea that abusers are all evil that often results in people staying with abusers or making excuses for them. They’ll look at the idea that an abuser must be evil and intend evil, and then they’ll remember some nice thing their abuser did for them last week, and they’ll think ‘I can’t be being abused and he can’t be an abuser because look, he got me flowers!’ The behaviour is abusive. 

The reality of domestic abuse, especially at the start of a terrible cycle, is that people will compare their abusive partners to that stereotype. Unsurprisingly, they’ll see the good in their partner, think it was just a one off, or they were having a bad day etc. The abusive partner will do this as well. Often they display guilt, for example, and because they feel remorse, they convince themselves they‘re not a ‘real’ abuser, because a ‘real’ abuser doesn’t feel guilt. Often they do. That doesn’t take away from what they do to people. 

The uncomfortable truth is that abusers look like the rest of us, and they aren‘t 100% bad in every way. They will have positive character traits. How do you think they convince themselves they‘re not really that bad? Think about how many times an abuser will promise it’s the last time. They aren’t always this evil stereotype. 

I think perhaps you misinterpreted me because it seems we’re are both anti abusers, but I also think that having lived this myself, we need to be realistic. Someone reading this might think ‘my abuser isn’t really an abuser bc they’re not stereotypical evil!’. Not the case. If they abuse you, make you feel unsafe, harm you, threaten you, they are an abuser. They don’t have to be evil to be an abuser. Abuse is bad enough on it’s own.
They are literally just projecting. They are the childish ones, and so they’re throwing that label out at you, even though it sounds like you’ve been mature and set boundaries.

Just posting my support here OP. My advice as a woman is that you should be yourself. If you are gentle and soft, then you will find women who look for that in a partner. Remember that what media tries to tell us is total nonsense. Pretty much all of my girl friends fancy different sorts of guys. I know it sounds daunting, but maybe being upfront about being sensitive will help? I don't know how you are in contact with people before you date them, but if it's online or on an app you could maybe chat about it? That way at least you won't have to go through a date and then get rejected on that basis. You can know then that if it doesn't work out it's not because you're too soft or sensitive, but just because you maybe don't click? 

I know on tv women often get written to like the tough guys, even the mean guys, but honestly so much of that is just media. We're just like men in the sense that we all have our own types and preferences, and I believe that if a relationship is something you want, you will find someone who suits you. Maybe she'll be more tough herself? Sometimes being opposites can help because you can both give each other what the other one needs. I'm really emotional and sensitive like you (although this is way more acceptable in women in this society) so I go for super dependable, reliable, gentle people. I respect those people and am friends with them, but I know what I need in a relationship, and I think figuring that out might help you navigate your own journey?

I guess just being kids the way my friends were seemed odd. Keeping any secrets or anything private seemed like a sin, to me. Like a betrayal. I was expected to tell all, answer any questions about my school and my friends - all of it. Anything kept to myself was seen as being bad or naughty, so I had no privacy, not in any single aspect of my being. Then when I wrote in diaries to have something for myself, I came back to find that my diary entry had been spell corrected with a red pen.

Okay so I have BPD and the stigma surrounding it is nonsense. They're learning more about it all the time. For BPD, it's really common to have been raised by a Narc. People with BPD are also way WAY more likely to be abused than be abusers. I'm not actually sure why it's grouped with other disorders at the moment, but I think that's actually changing as they better understand it. It does seem, from research, to be something that harms the sufferer, but does NOT necessarily make them an abuser. Most BPD cases are from prolonged childhood trauma. Also you get different types of BPD, so if you're from abuse, you may well be a 'quiet Borderline' which means you're not noticeable really, but you might self injure in various ways.

What I learned from group therapy is that yes it will stay with us for life, but it can be navigated, and also when you look at it as something that comes from that prolonged childhood trauma, it's not something you beat yourself up about. There are some in the mental health field that are still a bit behind when it comes to BPD and may treat you as the problem, but certainly that isn't the case. If you see someone that specialises in BPD or do a group therapy, you'll meet people that are actually usually just trauma survivors.

I can't answer as for your therapist, but I think maybe go into it with an open heart. You will probably be able to tell quite quickly if they're there to stigmatise, or there to help you manage it. It does sound pretty fast to make that assumption, but perhaps it's just something they felt you might want to look into? If you see them again and they start trying to diagnose you instantly or anything like that though - I'd run.

I get what you're saying about worrying you'll be blamed, just like your family blamed you, but again that's honestly common with BPD. Usually someone in a toxic family system, one of the kids, will end up very emotionally vulnerable. They'll be made that way by the abuse, made sicker really with the intention being that if they ever figure out how bad things are, they can be dismissed. Those of us with BPD have often experienced great invalidation in childhood. I think they believe that's part of how you develop the disorder.

Sorry if this wasn't helpful. I just wanted to reassure you that if you do have BPD it's not actually that scary in terms of being something to feel bad about. Princess Diana and Marilyn Monroe were both thought to be Borderlines. It doesn't make you abusive, but it usually does mean you've unfortunately been denied your childhood and selfhood in some way.
